subtopic: REPLY TO FAREWELL ADDRESS FROM BOTH HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT
REPLY TO FAREWELL ADDRESS FROM BOTH HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I have the honour to
inform the house that the Clerk has laid on the table to-day the reply of the Right Honourable the Earl of Athlone to the joint address of farewell presented to him by the Senate and the House of Commons, as follows:
Honourable members of the Senate,
Members of the House of Commons,
I thank you most sincerely for the; kind address of farewell which you have presented to me on the occasion of my approaching retirement as governor general of the Dominion of Canada.
It is with feelings of regret that I am concluding my official relationship as the representative of His Majesty the King in this country. It has been an honour and a great privilege to have served as governor general during the most eventful and calamitous years in the history of our time. The period of the war was fraught with innumerable difficulties many of which appeared at the time to be insurmountable. But parliament and the Canadian people, by their unselfish and untiring devotion to the cause of freedom, played a major part in the victorious struggle of the united nations against the implacable enemies of democracy.
My numerous tours of this vast country have enabled me to see almost every section of Canada.
I have been a witness of the efficiency, pel-severance and courage displayed by the men and women of Canada, whether they served in ' the armed forces or were engaged in factories or in one of the numerous societies which performed such miracles of organization and effectiveness. This ready response to the call of duty was an* evidence of the loyalty of the Canadian people to His Majesty the King and to the British commonwealth of nations, of which Canada is so important a part.
I am very much pleased to record that my relations with the members of both houses have been of the happiest.
I shall not fail, on my return to England, to convey to Their Majesties the King and Queen the loyal sentiments so admirably expressed in your address. It will be my pleasure also to convey to Queen Mary your kind remembrances. Her Majesty the Queen Mother has the warmest interest in the people of this country.
I join with you in expressing the hope that Their Royal Highnesses the Princess Elizabeth and the Princess Margaret may pay a visit to Canada in the near future.
On behalf of Princess Alice I wish to convey to you Her Royal Highness' appreciation for the very kind references you have made to her in your address. These have touched us both very deeply.
TMr. Pouliot.l
We shall never forget what Canada has contributed during the past six difficult and testing years. She earned the admiration and true gratitude of all free peoples for her magnificent and munificent contribution to the victorious prosecution of the war and to the welfare and rehabilitation of the suffering peoples of the world.
In bidding you farewell, Princess Alice and I wish to assure you of our deep and abiding affection and at the same time to express our complete confidence in the continued prosperity of Canada and the maintenance of her proud position as the senior dominion of the British commonwealth of nations.

I should like to supplement the statement I made in reply to the question asked yesterday by the leader of the opposition with reference to- a threatened stoppage of work on ships operating on the great lakes, by reading a letter addressed by myself to Mr. Sullivan on April 11. The letter reads as follows:
I have your letter of April 9 and there is a necessity in my opinion to record the facts up to date -as we understand them.
You met with me on March 25 and in addition to your committee, you will recall that Messrs. MacNamara and Maclean were present. The statement of myself and officials is that it was agreed that a telegram would be sent to the parties urging that a meeting take place on April 8 which was the earliest date convenient to you.
It was further stated that the meeting could be held in the Department of Labour office at Toronto if the parties so desired and also that a conciliation officer would be available if the parties asked for him.
In accordance with this understanding telegrams were dispatched to both parties and copies of same are attached.
It does seem to me that there is no room in the wording of the telegrams for any misunderstanding.
I am still of the opinion that it would have been advisable to meet with the operators. However, your committee decided otherwise.
You, of course, will at once agree that I could not, under the circumstances, say to the operators that they had refused to meet you.
It is noted that your executive has decided to take a strike vote beginning April 15 and I suggest to you that inasmuch as the process of collective bargaining between yourselves and the ship operators has not yet been concluded, a strike vote at the moment seems to be unnecessary and cannot be said to be in accordance with the provisions of the wartime labour relations regulations, P.C. 1003, which requires the parties to a dispute to bargain in good faith one with the other.
You may be assured that the department will do its utmost to bring about a mutually satisfactory agreement between the operators and

Labour Conditions
the employees. However, the department is still convinced that the most satisfactory solution would be one brought about by collective bargaining rather than by the passing of legislation providing for an eight-hour day.
I further wish to inform you that the labour department has requested the Department of Justice to review the relative authority as between the dominion and provincial governments and, in addition, the department has arranged for the submission of an independent legal opinion on this question.
Yours sincerely,
(sgd) Humphrey Mitchell
Has the minister considered calling these groups together in order to try to iron out this matter?

I have already done that. The operators are meeting on April 24 and I understand that a submission is to be made to the men's organization. It can be fairly stated that I have had some experience in labour negotiations, not only as chairman of boards of concilation but also as a negotiator for trade unions. I have never yet felt that anything is lost by negotiation. Sometimes when settlement of a dispute seems hopeless and a strike is inevitable the interested parties meet and in many instances an agreement is arrived at and work goes on unimpeded notwithstanding the difficult situation that existed.
May I give a word of advice to both sides? We have set up machinery for the settlement of disputes of this kind, and anybody who has a good case should never be afraid to come before an impartial tribunal. The machinery of the labour relations board-and I speak now from memory-has dealt with about 3,200 disputes. In only eight cases has there been a strike. I believe that is a fair average, and compared with other countries it gives an indication of the soundness of the legislation that this parliament has adopted for the settlement of disputes of this kind. I hope that good sense will be shown by both sides; that they will obey the law and use the machinery that most other organizations have used since the establishment of the code in this country.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
maintopic: REFERENCE IN DEBATE TO QUESTION OF PRICES
speechtext:
As a matter of privilege I should like to clarify a statement which was made the other evening and upon which there have been some reports that are creating some difficulties. Most of us find it rather difficult to get any butter in these days. Following my remarks the other evening the suggestion was made that I had said there might be a
further increase in the price of butter. Naturally that would cause persons who have butter to hold it for the higher price. I just wish to state that I had no intention of making any such suggestion either to this house or to the country, and I want to emphasize that fact. What I did was suggest that already there had been an increase in the price of butter and that there might be other products in connection with which increases might be necessary, but there was no reference to butter in the latter part of the statement.

1.	Have any representations been made to the government or to any Canadian delegation to the united nations organization in connection with the choice of Navy island as a permanent site for the headquarters of the united nations organization?
2.	If so, when and by whom were such representations made?
3.	What steps were taken by the government or the Canadian delegation as aforesaid to ensure that the permanent site of the united nations headquarters would be in Canada?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
1.	Yes.
2.	A number of representations were made at different times. Some of these were verbal. Those of which there is a record include the following:
By Mr. J. E. Lawson, on July 31;
By Mr. Davis Duff and Mr. Arthur A. Schmon, October 4, 1945;
By Senator J. J. Bench, December 31;
By Mr. Chauncey J. Hamblin and Mr. John A. Williamson, December 18.
In addition Mr. E. J. Anderson, Mr. Roy H. Davis and Mr. Louis Blake Duff brought this matter to the attention of the Canadian government and the Canadian delegation in London on a number of occasions.
3.	Action on the part of the Canadian government or any Canadian delegation to the united nations could not ensure that the permanent site for the headquarters of the uhited nations would be in Canada.
However, everything that could appropriately be done was done to ensure that the united nations should be aware of possible Canadian sites when giving consideration to the location of the permanent headquarters of the united nations. Representations concerning Navy island and other Canadian cities and localities were brought to the attention of the preparatory commission of the united nations. The preparatory commission circulated a list to delegations of possible sites, which included Navy island and other sites in Canada.
The preparatory commission decided that the permanent headquarters of the united nations should be located in the eastern part of the United States of America. A committee to make recommendations on the permanent site of the united nations was set up by the preparatory commission, and this committee sent an inspection group to the United States, with its terms of reference limited to specified areas around New York and Boston. The Canadian government made representations both in London and Washington with a view to having the united nations inspection group examine sites on the international boundary of the Niagara river.
The attitude of the Canadian government, like that of other member governments of the united nations, including the United States government, was that the choice of a permanent site was a matter for collective decision in the broad interests of the united nations.

['Then the hon. member's diagnosis is quite different from that of the majority of our citizens. We achieved so much under private enteiprise as to be the envy of the world. Was it government control that brought this country from the days of the pioneers to its present position? My conception is that we had better move along under the same policy under which we have operated from the beginning. It is my conception that the function of government is not to operate industry, but so to legislate that a favourable opportunity will be accorded free enterprise to invest its capital, thus giving employment and contributing to the financial needs of the nation.
Some hon. members bring up the hackneyed question of "no profits" operation. Those who imagine that the sole and only motive in our free enterprise is profit are singularly ignorant of human nature. No undertaking can thrive under persistent losses. No undertaking can thrive unless from time to time there is some profit in it. I fail to see why we cannot continue to depend on the same spirit of enterprise which, as I said before, has brought this country from the days of our pioneering forefathers up to the position which we hold to-day, when we have reached the peak of our industrial production.
Why is it that government cannot manage industry as economically as private enterprise' can? One reason is that under government management you cannot get the coordination and simplification and saving of time and effort that characterize private management. These are ideals that do not enter into government operation. The matter of losing a little time or a little effort does not enter so much into the minds of the government as it does into the minds of the businessman who is carrying on an enter-

prise of his own. There are exceptions, of course, but the conditions where you have these exceptions are not such as to satisfy the business executive. This lack of coordination, lack of simplification and saving of time and effort is not applicable alone to public ownership in Canada. It applies also in the United States. Nor is it peculiar to our generation. It is a condition that is natural to government service, but it is unnatural in private business. You will always find under government control what businessmen characterize as red tape, seniority or some such thing, which you do not find under private enterprise. I contend, therefore, that it is not wise for the people of Canada to turn over to the government to do the things which they themselves can accomplish.
Wise leaders in governments to-day are telling businessmen things that they should know. They are telling them that they have a national duty beyond the bounds of their own enterprise and that if they will step into it and do their public duty it will not be necessary for the government to take over so many projects for which it is not fitted. I am strongly convinced that individual enterprise and freedom of contract is the policy that should be followed in this country if we are to maintain and develop Canada. This is not the day of revolution either in industry or in any other effort. It is the day of evolution. Let is try to improve the policies and methods we have followed from the beginning. I do not see that we the Canadian people are suffering at all from the rheumatic pains of old age. I believe that we are suffering from the growing pains of fast and successful development. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I cannot support this resolution. I think it is a move in the wrong direction.']

speakeroldname: Mr. CLARENCE GILLIS (Cape Breton South) moved:
speechtext:
Whereas private enterprise in the development of the mineral resources of Canada has not operated in the best interests of all of the people of Canada either in time of peace or in time of war;
Therefore be it resolved that, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of bringing the developed and undeveloped mineral resources of Canada under government control land operation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have been waiting to discuss this resolution for the past five years. I am sorry that this afternoon, on the eve of a house adjournment, and perhaps at a time when a great deal of government business remains to be done, I have to initiate a discussion which I believe deals. with a matter of urgent importance to the people of Canada.
The resolution suggests that I should be free to discuss all mineral resources in Canada. I can assure hon. members that a discussion as broad as that would require some considerable time. Therefore in the time at my disposal this afternoon I shall confine my remarks chiefly to the coal mining industry of Nova Scotia. I assume that hon. members from other parts of Canada who represent constituencies in which coal mining operations are carried on will take advantage of this opportunity to place the position of the industry on record in the house.
I believe I am safe in saying that the remarks I shall make with reference to the industry in Nova Scotia will be applicable to the whole of industry across the country. The coal mining industry is a very sick one at the present time. It has been indicated in the house on many occasions that employment.
m
Mineral Resources
A good minister.

-made some pertinent remarks in the legislature within the last couple of weeks. I notice that the Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) has said that he is a good minister. I hope, then, that my hon. friend will support what the Minister of Industry and Publicity in the Nova Scotia government had to say respecting the mining industry of that province.
I will support every good cause.

Federal action is necessary for the rehabilitation of this industry. If subsidizing the coal industry of this country was any solution under the system of free enterprise the Nova Scotia mining industry should be a very prosperous industry to-day because it has been heavily subsidized. However, the fact of the matter is that that industry is in a worse position to-day than at any time in its history. The minister of industry acting for the Nova Scotia government, tabled a report in the legislature for the year ending November 30, 1945. At that time he said that too much emphasis could not be placed upon the deplorable position of the coal industry of that province. He stated further that the total production for the last fiscal year was only 5,170,400 short tons, a decrease of 637,710 tons from the production of 1944. This was the lowest figure since 1902. The production per man fell to 1-58 tons.
IMr. Gillis.]
These figures take on an even more alarming aspect when considered against the background of the 1944 report. In the 1044 report the minister referred to the lamentable decrease in the total production from the previous year. The production per man shift in 1944 was 1-66 short tons, the lowest rate since 1900 and the lowest rate for which statistics are available.
That is 1944?

1944. He was comparing the 1945 report with the 1944. The total production and man-shift production in 1945 dropped below the 1944 figure. Despite the fact, as the Minister of Reconstruction well knows, that the federal government came to the rescue of private enterprise in the operation of this industry, and has been practically carrying the financial load of the continued operation, the industry continues to go down. This suggests to my mind tljat the time has come when the federal government, in the interests of the taxpayers of Canada, should accept some responsibility in the operation of this industry. In his report the minister went on to outline some of the disabilities under which the industry operates. He stated that all signs pointed to the fact that the loss in production was attributable not so much to the physical conditions in the industry as to human relations. He said a great change must take place in the attitude of all concerned if the industry was to retain its former place in the provincial economy.
That is the opinion of the minister of industry in the Nova Scotia government. The question is one which should concern not only the people of Nova Scotia but hon. members of this house, particularly the Nova Scotia members. It would be difficult to exaggerate the gravity of the situation as revealed in the formal language and hard statistics of the official report.
I do not raise this question in spirit of fault-finding or recrimination. I do it more to focus the attention of the government on the problem in order that they may t^ke some constructive action to see that this industry is not blotted out. It is the responsibility of the governments, provincial and federal, who are the custodians of the natural resources of the country and who have been providing funds, for the last five years at least, in order that this industry may continue to function.
As I said at the beginning, if private enterprise and the system of subsidizing industry were any solution, the problem would not be as acute as it is to-day. They have had a fair trial in the mining industry and in my opinion

Mineral Resources
that industry has failed completely to meet the needs of this country, both in times of war and in times of peace. To-day the government is underwriting the losses of this industry and is acting as their sales agents. In my opinion it is the duty and responsibility of the government to take over the industry, reorganize it and operate it as a government enterprise. The government is paying the bills anyway.
As hon. members know-and this is particularly within the knowledge of the Minister of Reconstruction-there is a royal commission now probing the whole mining industry across the country. This commission will cost the taxpayers of Canada a considerable amount of money, but in my opinion it will be money well spent. I know some of the personnel of that commission, and I am reasonably sure that when its report is made we shall have for the first time a realistic picture of the coal mining industiy across Canada.
Regardless of what this commission may find, or what its recommendations to the minister may be, I am convinced that there is no solution for the problems facing the coal industry unless the federal government take it over and operate it in the interests of the people of Canada. I believe the mining industry of Nova Scotia is in much the same position to-day as was the mining industry of Great Britain up to the time the British government took it over and operated it. The workers in the industry in Nova Scotia have lost confidence in those who operate the industry. In Great Britain there were many independent operators, whereas in Nova Scotia it is a straight monopoly. This makes it all the more necessary for the federal government to step in and reexamine the whole setup on the basis of the commission's findings.
The government should consider the advisability of nationalizing the coal industry of Canada, particularly that of Nova Scotia. This government should follow the mechanics employed by the British government. The matter was studied in that country for a long time and discussed on many occasions in the British House of Commons. The men who laid down the mechanics of taking over the industry in Great Britain had long experience, and we should do well to study what was done over there. I believ6 the time is not far distant when the government will have to take this step.
A national board should be set up consisting of men with the necessary experience and qualifications. It should function under a separate minister who would be responsible to parliament for tjie operation of the industry. In addition there should be two regional
boards in Nova Scotia, one on the mainland! and one on the island of Cape Breton. While the national board would consist of experts-working under the direction of the minister,, in order to get the active cooperation of the workers the regional boards should consist of equal representation of management and the workers, so that they could work out the-basic problems that exist underground and enable the national board to get a complete-picture of the operation.
In addition to the two boards which would! manage the industry under the minister's direction there should be set up, -as was done in Great Britain, an industrial coal consumers' council. This council is responsible for processing and marketing, and for making contacts with the industry and acting as sales agent in the marketing of coal; it also fixes prices in conjunction with the national board.
In addition there is what is known as a domestic coal consum'ers' council, which acts as sales agent in the domestic field in the processing and marketing of coal, all under the direction of the national board.
In my opinion, if these simple steps were taken in this country under the direction of a minister like the Minister of Reconstruction, who in matters of this kind is very realistic, who is an engineer and likes to get things done, much could be done. I should like to see him in charge of that kind of set-up, and I am certain that the steps that I have mentioned will have to be taken if the province of Nova Scotia is to survive. Either that or an emigration policy from Nova Scotia to other parts of Canada will be necessary.
One of the government's officials, the Hon. Michael Dwyer, who is maritime director of selective service, addressing a commercial club in Halifax not so long ago, stated that on the average for many years fifteen hundred young people had left the province of Nova Scotia every year to go to the United States or other parts of Canada to seek employment. The war has brought us no relief from that situation. Indeed, the employment situation in Nova Scotia to-day is fifty per cent worse than it was in 1939. On the island of Cape Breton alone there are over 4,500 registered unemployed, of whom 1,500 are ex-service men who never did a day's work in their lives, who went from the street into the army apd through the war and are now back on the street. Many other service personnel in that part of the country are not registered, because so long as they are receiving their out-of-work benefits they do not go through that channel. The consequence is that a serious unemployment situation is developing in Nova Scotia which will have to be dealt


with very soon. The basis of it all is the coal-mining industry, and there can be no relief under your system of free enterprise, because to rehabilitate that industry will require a large amount of capital expenditure. As lion, members who sat on the reconstruction committee with myself in 1942, 1943 and 1944, will remember, the heads of the Dominion Steel and Coal company, when questioned as to their plans for the future, the making of new openings and further mechanization of the mines already developed, stated frankly that it would cost a lot of money and that they were not going to spend the money to make those developments; but if the federal government would make the capital available, yes, they would go to work. If the federal government would do that, I am sure that there are some profits to be made in that industry. If a proper valuation of the industry were made it would be found that perhaps fifty per cent of the stock is watered. Let the minister take that industry over and squeeze the water out of the stock, fix wage rates and the selling price of coal on the basis of the costs involved, and then I am sure the coal can be marketed economically and that new openings can be made for employment in Nova Scotia. This step must be taken if the industry is to survive.
Every government in Canada is responsible for the situation in the coal mining industry to-day because they have been the custodian of that resource in every part of Canada. All our minerals were placed in the ground by the Lord, and they belong to the people. No one has any right to exploit mineral resources for private gain. Those who have operated those resources for private gain in the past have taken out the coal that was easiest to get out of the ground and got as much out of it as they could in the way of profits. Shack communities were built around the mines where the miners had to live under deplorable conditions, in every section of the mining industry all across Canada. Go to Minto, New Brunswick, and see how the miners live and work in that area. The conditions there are not peculiar to New Brunswick; the same is true of Nova Scotia. Towns which a few years ago were prosperous communities are now nothing but ghost towns. Hundreds of thousands of dollars were invested in the building of churches and schools and halls in these communities, and to-day they are falling down. Those who were operating the mines extracted as much profit as they could out of the industry, faulty mining practices were carried on, the resources were destroyed, and now these communities, in which hundreds of thousands of dollars were
I Mr. Gillis.J
invested by the people who lived here, are falling down, while those who drew most of the money out of the industry live up in Westmount, Montreal, in beautiful mansions. They never saw that industry and know nothing about it. They were merely interested in getting what they could out of it. In the meantime the workers were left to slave underground and live under the conditions I have described, conditions which no one here would tolerate. The smokeless smoke-stacks in these ghost towns in Nova Scotia and other parts of Canada are a grim monument to those who have been sent here for the last twenty-five years to make our laws. They are an indictment against us.
In my opinion the time has come for the federal government, recognizing the fact that the provincial governments have fallen down on the job of managing that particular industry, to step in and take it over and put it on its feet. If the mechanics as set up in Britain to-day for the nationalization of the coal industry were adopted here, under a realistic minister who wants to get things done, I am sure that the industry in Nova Scotia could be put back on its feet and occupy its proper place in the economy of the province.
There is another thought that I would leave with the house. We must consider the coal resources of this country as a potential supply of fuel oil requirements in the future. I read an article just a few days ago, written by a Toronto university professor, who pointed out that the fuel oil supplies on this North American continent were running out and that with the terrific developments in air transport we would have to turn to the coal resources of this country to meet the requirements of air transportation in the future. That is a long story and a technical one and I shall not go into it this afternoon. I just leave the thought with the members of the government who will be examining the report of the royal commission when it is brought down.
There has been criticism that the commission has taken too long in making its inquiry and report. Personally I am not concerned as to the length of time it takes. I want it to take all the time that is necessary to do a real job. When the commission brings down its report it will be the duty of the members of this house, particularly those from coal-mining areas, to study it closely and to press the federal government for action as soon as possible to preserve and develop our coal resources.
The minister of industry in Nova Scotia pointed out that the major disability from

Mineral Resources
which the industry was suffering was labour relations. I know something about that, and there is a lot in what he says. This labour relations question goes back forty years, when there was terrific opposition to unions in Nova Scotia. Miners were thrown out one hundred per cent from the company houses and lived for nine or ten months in the basements of churches, in tents, all over the country, simply because they wanted to form a union. They were gaoled by the hundreds. The federal government sent in the army, the navy and cavalry, and barbed-wired the province-
What about the air force?

They were not organized at that time. This was done at the request of the mining magnates of Canada. That is why there is this bit of resentment; they remember th^se things. The sons of the men who went through this experience feel that the attitude of the bosses of steel and coal has changed very little. Under a government owned set-up I believe this picture would change. Knowing the miners of Nova Scotia as I do, I believe they would feel that they were working for themselves.
I can tell my hon. friend that it has not changed the situation in Great Britain.
It has not? The minister has not followed the British Hansard.

Oh, yes. I have been
reading about it.

Besides, I Would not expect
the situation in this country to change in four or five months. It is a job which would take a little time. But if I were still in those coal mines and I found a federal government which had the courage to face up to this problem, I would say that I was working now for myself, and that I had equal responsibility with the government of this country in that they were honestly trying to rehabilitate the industry, get down to brass tacks, increase production, and do everything they could to put the industry on its feet.
Make no mistake about it: the miners at our end of the country know this problem better, perhaps, than anyone else. In their brief to the royal commission which sat in Sydney when it began its work, the miners of Nova Scotia strongly emphasized the necessity of nationalization of that industry. They have no illusions. They have had boards and commissions for thirty years, but nothing came out of it. It was the same old story: pour more money into the coffers of Dominion Steel and
Coal, another deficit for them to show at the end of the year as a plea that "we can't pay wages, we can't fix our houses, we can't do anything but sit tight, put pressure on the federal government and squeeze more money out of them." Not a sales agent in the field, but send a wire to Ottawa for new markets and get a delegation of citizens to go there to plead for them. The government has pap-fed them so long now that they sit back and consider themselves your baby, and you continue to hand them the milk-bottle. The industry to-day is completely inefficient and mismanaged, simply because the federal government has given them the money necessary to increase their depreciation at the end of the year, to put money in the reserve fund and to juggle profits from one subsidiary to the other.
I should like to see as quickly as possible ' the federal government take that industry over, set up the boards I have mentioned, ask the cooperation of the miners of Nova Scotia in putting the industry back on its feet, get a proper valuation of it, squeeze the water out of the stock, and zone the markets of this country that are fairly economical in so far as their industry is concerned. In my opinion if these things were done the labour relations would improve. I believe you can make money in this industry. It is one of our greatest natural resources; it has to be maintained'; but I cannot see why the taxpayers of this country should spend millions of dollars a year in subsidizing an industry where the head of the company draws an annual salary of $100,000, another fellow draws a salary of $75,000 a year, and so all the way down the line; and they spend four or five months every year down in Florida fanning themselves with a panama "under the bamboo tree." That kind of person is not necessary. The taxpayers of Canada should not pay such salaries to people who have badly mismanaged one of our greatest resources.
I am going to conclude by urging the federal government to take the necessary steps to give back to the people of Canada a resource which belongs to them, which was deeded over to private interests without asking the people anything about it, which has been badly mismanaged under the system of free enterprise, which has gone down to nothing, which as far as the federal government is concerned has been on relief for the last twenty-five years. It is time the federal government took it over and earnestly considered restoring it to the people, putting it back on its feet, making what money can be made from it and passing the returns back to the people of the industry and the people of Canada in the way of social services.

May I ask the hon. member a question, purely as a matter of information, and quite aside from the merit of the argument he has been making with respect to taking over these mines?
Certainly.

The hon. member gave the figure of the production per man per day of coal as being 1-66 tons last year and T58 at present. Can he tell us what the average production per man is in Great Britain, and also in some of the better mines of the United States-^just as a matter of information.
Yes. They are away above that.
Has the hon. member the figures?
I have not the actual figures here, but speaking from memory, the United States production is away up, about three times as much.

It is about seven tons a day. I can give the approximate figure. I am speaking from memory, but I do not think I am far out. It is down now to almost a ton per man per day in Great Britain. It is just over seven tons in. the United States, and I think it is a fraction over three tons in western Canada. Of course there is a reason for this disparity, a reason it is quite easy to give. Mining in the United States is somewhat different. You get there the strip operations and open pits.
What was the most production per man in the more favourable days in Nova Scotia?

It was up around three or
four tons. Of course as far as Great Britain is concerned the explanation is that their mines are worked out. They are old seams; they are submarine; they are difficult, and the further you go into them the longer your hauls, so your production per man per day necessarily drops.
And the same applies here?

The same applies in Nova Scotia. New openings are necessary in Nova Scotia. Conditions in the United States, of course, are not comparable at all. It is a straight mechanized electrified proposition. In many instances they just run a steam shovel in the side of a mountain and shovel out the coal. .
Or they strip the seam.

Or they strip the seam. The grand average is taken for the industry. Conditions here are less favourable. Nevertheless this is one of our great natural resources and we have to take it as it is. This is the way we shall have to do it. The economy of the province is based on coal. Either you have got to rehabilitate it and put it on its feet, or you must start to move the people of Nova Scotia out of that province. I am reasonably sure that with a proper capital investment and a few new openings in Nova Scotia the industry can be rehabilitated. But you are not going to get that capital investment from the present operators.

I certainly appreciate the opportunity which has been given to the House of Commons to speak on mining in general. I was surprised to some extent by what I heard from the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), although I must praise him for bringing forward so forcibly the situation of the section of the mining industry in which his province and indeed the whole of Canada is vitally interested, namely coal mining. But I know he will realize that I am not digressing if I discuss mining in general, including gold mining, in which my own section is more particularly interested.
Before I go further, however, may I say that I believe I sense in the remarks of the mover of this resolution something a little milder than might have been heard two or three years ago. I read some of the propaganda which was made by the Socialist party in Great Britain during the general election last fall. Speaking of the question of nationalization of coal mines in Great Britain, the supporters of that party were not backward in telling the British electors that if they were put into power the coal problem would be settled immediately. It was pleasing indeed to me this afternoon when the hon. member for Cape Breton South realized and recognized that it might take some time, even some years, to settle the problems of the coal mining industry in Canada. This surely applies to Great Britain also. At one time the British electors were led to believe that the moment the party got into power the question would be solved immediately.
No.

I want to complete my thought. It is always easier to theorize and criticize when you have not the responsibility of government. I say that without any bitterness of spirit or any idea of criticism. Our friends of the C.C.F. have that experience in Saskatchewan to-day. In the distant future

Mineral Resources
they may have it in Canada. They may have the responsibility of government. They may theorize at the present time on problems that seem easy of solution, but they may find them awfully hard to solve when they have the responsibility of office.
I read British periodicals and papers of Conservative and Socialist inclinations. Even* to-day the British consumers and the British people generally are far from satisfied with the coal situation. The government, through Mr. Attlee, the Prime Minister, and some of his ministers, have told the people, and rightly so, to be patient. They have asked them to endure the same sacrifices that they experienced during the war. In that they are right again. I make this statement deliberately. We all realize that it is much easier to make promises than to fulfil them the moment a party gets into power. I do not say that as an alibi for the shortcomings of my own party. They have been in power for a long time, and the}' realize the heavy responsibilities that fall not only upon the shoulders of the government and the representatives of the party in the house but also upon the shoulders of parliament.
I want to compliment the hon. member for Cape Breton South on presenting so eloquently and warmly the case for the coal miners and the coal mining industry in general. However, to him the solution is lamentably simple, and that applies to his party generally. Of course we are used to that in the House of Commons.
During the debate on the speech from the throne an amendment was proposed by the historical-it is not historical now; it is too new a party for that-Progressive Conservative party. The amendment suggested that it was possible to solve all the problems, of Canada by following some of the policies of the Progressive Conservative party. Then there was a subamendment brought forward and ably presented by the C.C.F. party. Their formula was the simplest one possible: all you had to do was to socialize all industries and all activities in Canada. If that were done you would have a new earthly paradise as far as this country was concerned. All problems would be solved. Later on the able leader of the Social Credit party introduced a subamendment. They are sincere also in their proposals. I studied their policies. I even studied their basic dividends, which none of my relatives in Alberta ever received, although the party promised that it would be the solution of all problems. To their way of thinking the, amendment they offered would solve all the problems of this country. It would be done by one simple amendment, 63260-62
one simple gesture. It does not work that way, Mr. Speaker. In my opinion that is one of the weaknesses of democracy.
I was speaking to some fine young men and women the day before yesterday in my office, -the youth movement. I said to them: "As Canadians are you ready to make the sacrifices that the Russian people are called upon to make at the present time for their government and for their country?" In Canada we apparently do not appreciate the benefits of democracy. Generally speaking we are ready and willing to take all the benefits, but very few of us are ready and willing to accept the necessary sacrifices to make it a going concern.
If we have a socialist government next year, or ten years from now, that government will soon find out the solution does not lie in a simple socialist formula.
What is the import of the resolution? It reads as follows:
Whereas private enterprise in the development of the mineral resources of Canada has not operated in the best interests of all of the people of Canada either in time of peace or in time of war;
Therefore be it resolved that, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of bringing the developed and undeveloped mineral resources of Canada under government control and operation.
This is a far-reaching resolution. If it were approved by parliament it would mean that all Canadians would be led and governed by the government. If you socialize the mineral resources of the country you must of necessity, in my opinion, include all the industries. If my hon. friends are sincere, if they want to go the whole show, as they may some day, they would put a resolution on the order paper calling for the socialization of land. One step leads to the other. You cannot socialize mining, you cannot single out one industry without socializing the whole, the manufacturing industries and so forth. The next step would be socialized farming.
To my way of thinking there is no simple remedy, no one formula to solve the problem. Democracy, as we understand it and practise it in this country and as it is practised in some parts of Europe, learns by its shortcomings and by its errors, and by constructive criticism and by speeches such as we had this afternoon. Through these processes it finds the solution to some of the big problems that have to be faced at the present time. Those problems will never be solved by appealing to demagoguery and promising a new heaven on earth.
One thing I deplore in intelligent and capable people is that for purely political reasons they find it advisable to decry Canada, to

Mineral Resources

speak of other countries, such as Sweden, which we all respect, to speak of countries such as Norway, Australia, New Zealand and so forth, telling us that they are away ahead of us and much better countries in which to live. So far as I am concerned I am satisfied to live in Canada. I think it is the best country under the sun. You will never have a human system which is absolutely perfect. We shall never solve our problems by appeals to passion and promising pie in the sky. During the last federal election in my section of the country we had two fine C.C.F. candidates, one in Temis-kaming and the other in Cochrane. One of them was a high-school teacher, a well-qualified, highly-respected citizen. The other was a prosperous pharmacist from Kirkland Lake. Every time I listened to their speeches on the radio I found that they never had a word of praise for their own country. I said to the people of my constituency: "Where is the Canadianism of these two men? Surely there must be something good in Canada. At some time, either in the not distant past or in the near future, there will be something that Canadians should be proud of." But never, never at any time, did they find it possible to utter a word of praise for what Canada had been doing. It was always a country some thousands of miles away from Canada which they praised. They never gave a bit of credit to their own country. I am not speaking politically when I say that, because they did not give any credit to the Liberal party; but at least they could have given some credit to the Canadian people who live here, who want to make it a bigger and better country. These were the only objections I had to <their campaign. I have no advice- to give to any party, but I do not believe in pessimism. I believe in optimism. I believe in a reformed progressive capitalistic system.
I come from a section of the country where we have been fighting the elements, fighting with nature, where you run by yourself with very little help from any government. We want the country to do as much as it possibly can. It will be no solution to the coal mining problem of Canada for the government to take it over overnight. To my mind the solution would be the finest cooperation possible between the federal and provincial governments, the unions and the owners of these mines. They are all Canadians and they want to build up this country.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South used the old cliche that somebody gets $100,000 a year. He knows quite well that nobody
[Mr. Bradette.J
gets $100,000 a year without the Minister of Finance taking seventy-five per cent of it. Then he used the old cliche of their going down to Florida and fanning their faces with a panama hat. I know he wants to be fair. I had to send some of my poor relatives to Florida and I had to go into debt on account jof it, but they went down for their health. People do not always go there for pleasure. I deplore any such luxuries and extravagances 'also, but I do not believe it is fair to group together all the people who happen to be owners and say they are all doing these things, while the fact is that most of them are trying their best to make this a bigger and better Canada. I do not think it is fair to try to make others believe these people are not playing the game with the workers of their particular section of the country. I am making these statements sincerely; I know we are going' through strenuous times, but I repeat that these problems will never be solved by any such simple formula.
I could tell the house of perhaps three or four mine owners in my own section of Canada who have been practically a disgrace to the country, and who have done harm to its economy and to the capitalistic system; but they form an infinitesimal minority. Where you get one of these men acting in that way you have hundreds or thousands of others who play the game with everyone. I well remember travelling with a member of the C.C.F. party when the war expenditures committee went to Sault Ste. Marie. I am sure he was quite sincere when te told me, "I realize that to-day no man could become president of a corporation like that purely by accident." Surely it is not fair to this parliament to try to make people believe that because a person happens to be a mine owner or a mine president he is dissipating in California or Florida, or something like that. I resent such statements. They will not help this country generally. I know our hearts go out to those who suffer. I have every sympathy with the miners mentioned by the hon. member for Cape Breton South, just as I have sympathy for my own people if they do not receive justice. I have spent weeks and months at a time with my own men in the lumber camps, to see that they received the consideration they deserved.
Was the hon. member subsidized by the government when he was doing that?
Subsidized for what?

When you were doing this work about which you are speaking?

Oh, no, I did that on my own, as the member for my riding and as a citizen of this country. I thought it was my duty to stay with the men, to go with them to the camps to see what the living conditions were, in order that anything that was wrong might be rectified. But if I had gone before these men and said, "Yes, you should keep on striking because the general manager of the Spruce Falls mill is getting $40,000 a year," for instance, would that have helped the situation? Would that have helped these men? Not at all. We went to these higher authorities and told them both the wages and the working conditions were unsatisfactory, and in most cases we won our points.
I am speaking sincerely on this subject, because I believe my constituency is one of the greatest gold mining centres in Canada, if not on the north American continent. I will not mention the names of the men who are at the head of these gold mines, but the hon. member for Cape Breton South was there last winter; no doubt he met some of them and spoke with them, and he must have been struck with their humanitarianism. The homes of most of these general superintendents are open day and night to any of the men; not their offices but their homes. They have made mistakes at times, because, after all, they are human, but they have tried to rectify those mistakes.
I was not talking about superintendents, because, after all, they are workers too. I am talking about the fellow who lives in Westmount, in Montreal, and who does not see the mine.

Well, you go and speak to these men in Westmount. They will tell you they are workers too. Everyone is working in his own way. We cannot all have the same occupation. We are working as members of parliament, sitting here this afternoon discussing the problems of the moment. We call ourselves workers. Men who work in the bush or on the drive would say we were having a wonderful time, not doing anything. You cannot apply the same standard to every walk of life, to all the activities of human beings. I do not make that statement with any feeling, because I repeat that I appreciate the fact that the hon. member has brought the situation of the coal mining industry of Canada to the attention of this country. In our section we are far away from the coal mines, and naturally we have to pay high prices for the coal we use in our industries.
Let me give the house another example of what public ownership has done in my part of the country. Twenty-five or thirty years ago some fine old prospectors-and God bless them; they are doing wonderful work for this country-found a great lignite field in northern Ontario. Immediately they came to our section they raised money among themselves; they went back again to stake the land and so on. Then, and I do not say this in a critical way because I believe it was done with the very best intentions, Hon. Charles McCrea, an outstanding man who was in Mr. Ferguson's cabinet, expropriated that lignite field without any compensation at all to those of us who had put money into it. Very high, hopes were entertained that the government was going to see that the lignite field would be worked and exploited for the benefit of the people. That was over twenty-five years ago, but I do not believe we have seen more than three or four tons of that lignite coal. In connection with that field there has been more political gerrymandering than I have ever seen anywhere else. All governments have to take some blame for that situation, because they all went in and made an awful mess of it. I maintain that if private interests had been allowed to invest capital and take a chance there, as we do in our own mining section, the needs of northern Ontario to-day would be largely supplied from that lignite field. I am sure the Ontario members who are listening to me will agree with that statement.
Talk about public ownership of mines! We all remember the old, historic town of Cobalt, where silver mining boomed for many years. When it was at its peak the Ontario government, again with the best of intentions, expropriated one of these mines which was to be run by the government. What happened? Prior to being expropriated that mine was showing a fine surplus each year. After being operated by the Ontario government, for a year and a half it had such large deficits they had to close up the mine and get out of the mining business.
I give these examples in order that the "house may realize the exact situation. I repeat that I think there is only one solution of the problems of the coal mining industry, which is so vital to our economy; and that solution is not an easy one. We realize that with all the coal we have in the east and the west most of our industries in southern Ontario have to use coal brought from Pennsylvania; and that applies even more forcibly to northern Ontario. It is true that coal has no nationality, and we have to do this because of transportation costs and also,
Mineral Resources

in many instances, because of the quality of the coal we must buy. So that if we are ever to solve the coal problem, of which my hon. friend spoke so eloquently, we must find some method by which it will be possible to get that fine Nova Scotia coal to both southern and northern Ontario. If that could be done we would be your best customers and would readily buy all that coal we could use in order to help the miners of Nova Scotia and strengthen the whole national economy of this country.
I have mentioned mining in general. I offer no excuse if for a few moments I speak of the gold mining of my own section, with which I am more familiar. Many people think gold mining is such a bonanza that one can put in a dollar and after a year or two be worth a million dollars. I know my hon. friends from Nipissing and Temiskaming, and others who have invested money in gold mining operations, have always come out losers. I know I have been a loser all the way through.
You should be a promoter.

I must say to the hon. member that with all the regulations we have from Toronto, even promoters do not always come out on the right side. We have at Queens Park some fine, well trained watchdogs. It is true that sometimes, through Ducket-shop practices, some people may be fleeced, but that was never done with official sanction, whether we had a Progressive, a Conservative or a Liberal government in office. Ehey have always tried to play fair with everybody. The gold mining industry means a great deal to our national economy, but it is highly speculative. I wish I could put on record how many people are making money in it, and how many people are always showing deficits. As hon. members all know, personal initiative means a very great deal in connection with gold mining, silver mining, nickel mining, or any metal mining development. No doubt many hon. members listening to me this afternoon have met prospectors, * both old and young. How keen these men are; how they love their jobs. Could you visualize putting these men into government service as civil servants? Could you visualize a young prospector, who has his heart in the north country, being told, "Now, we are going to put you under a civil service organization. You are going to be allowed to go to this territory only so many days or so many weeks. Then you must come back and report." You could never have any real prospecting under such conditions.
But the government is sending them out now.

Oh, no, not now. They are sending expert men to make a map geology analysis of the whole country, to show prospectors, promoters and others who may be interested the possibility of undertaking new ventures. Surely my hon. friends do not want to create the impression that this government has a special department of prospectors, who prospect for and promote the mines they find? It does not work out in that way. Again I say that the minute you make a businessman a civil servant for the rest of his life, just at that moment you lose most of his qualifications and ability for personal initiative.
You release him from bondage. You take him out of the hands of the companies.

The word "bondage"
may have different significance in different places. It sounds as though the hon. member wishes to create the impression that we in the north country are in the relationship of masters and slaves.

The hon. member mentioned prospectors. I said that the government all through this war and even at .the present time have sent prospectors out all over the country, grub-staking them and financing them. Then, when they found something they had to come back and turn it over to one of the mining companies. Why not turn it over to the government?
It was done under war conditions.
They are still doing it.

Not on a large scale. To prove what I say, I shall place before the house some of the features about mining, particularly in my own section of the country. Prospecting for new minerals at the present time in Canada has all but ceased and, if the mining industry is to continue on any worthwhile basis, this unfortunate situation must be corrected immediately. Emphasizing the necessity for quick action is the fact that under war-time demands for maximum metal production, coupled with a labour shortage, development work at producing mines has been necessarily and drastically curtailed, and ore reserves are being dissipated at an accelerated pace.
We have all heard of Mr. LaBine, who went away up into the north country, into the far north, which most of the Canadian people knew nothing about. Most people thought it was too far away; they really did

Mineral Resources
not realize how far it was-up in the Great Bear lake district. But what a great thing it was for the world when there were found pitchblende, the ore from which radium is derived, and uranium.
Would that have been done under the civil service? Would it have been done by men who were paid by the government at so much an hour or so much a day? Great sacrifices were made by the men who went there. At the present time we have hundreds of young men in my section of the country-men from Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, men from every centre of population in Canada. Those men are preparing themselves, equipping themselves, to go into the wilderness, in among the flies and in the rain and bad weather, where they will have none of the comforts of life.
Why do they do it? They do it because they believe in private enterprise. They do it because they believe that to a certain extent we should work out our own salvation. Can we visualize their working for any government, provincial, municipal or federal, and working under those conditions? Can we visualize their asking for two or three months leave to do prospecting work of that kind? This applies to all walks of life.
I for one, of French descent, can never visualize the British people being absolutely tied down under the yoke of socialism or Marxism. The British empire, as we know it, would never have developed or would never have been built under a principle of socialism, because socialism simply means this, that the individual loses his identity. That would, generally speaking, be absolutely repugnant to the British people. Without trying to prophesy, I am certain that never in Great Britain, even under a so-called socialistic government will they have absolute state socialism. That is my belief, so far as that country is concerned.
This brings up some strange things. I wish the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) were in his seat at the moment. He made certain references the other day to the royal family which, perhaps, I shall have another occasion to mention.
Some people are inclined to the view that the mining industry generally is making large profits. I well remember the days when Viscount Bennett was prime minister of this country. At that time, ignoring the advice of an able minister from my northern section of the country, a gentleman who was then minister of labour, Hon. Wesley Gordon, a bullion tax was put on gold. It was thought that this would be good policy, and that it would be a popular move. But the first thing he knew, not only did he have the mining
interests coming to Ottawa with their protests, but in addition ne had the prospectors. He had the investors, the retailers, the wholesalers, the manufacturers-all of them were coming here and telling him it was a mistake. After a few months the government was honest enough to withdraw [DOT] that bullion tax-Yes, it looked good on paper, because people-are always thinking in terms of profits of gold', mining or nickel mining; but it did not work out in practice.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South has shown, and rightly so, that the coal mining industry at the present time is not in a; position to produce all it should, or to permitworking conditions which should be permitted.-That bullion tax was taken away because it would destroy the initiative of those connected with mining operations.
I have no doubt that everyone is interested in gold mining in this country. I can well remember the hon. member who formerly represented the constituency of Grey-Bruce, Miss Agnes Macphafl, being invited to speak at the commencement exercises which took place in the vocational school at Timmins. In her opening remarks she said, "You are a strange people up here in the north country. You sweat and work day and night all your lives to extract these things from the earth; then you ship it down to our section of the country and we bury it in the ground." Then George Drew-not the premier of Ontario, but another George Drew, who was mayor of Timmins- said this to Miss Macphail: "Well, what you say is possibly true. But I understand you come from a section of the country where you produce large quantities of tobacco. Up here we buy that .tobacco at fair prices-sometimes at high prices-and turn it into ashes and smoke." This shows that in a national economy there is a necessity for all manner of activities which may be found within the boundaries of a country.
Regardless of what some of my Social Credit friends may say, there is a sound reason for gold mining in Canada. If that industry were denied to the country, we wTould realize what a tremendous influence it has had. For instance, in my own section alone there are tens of thousands of people who are interested and employed in gold mining. More than that, we have always a ready market for our product. Surely we should be the last to destroy a community which has that gold production. Indeed, the whole world seems to have been satisfied with the find which was made in South Africa only a few days ago.
So that it shows there is no special privilege given to this industry. There was a member in the house at one time who represented one
Mineral Resources

of the Winnipeg seats-I believe it was Mr. Heaps, who is now in the government employ- who discussed the bullion tax, and referred to gold mining as a sheltered industry. I rose in my place immediately and said that there was certainly no shelter so far as gold mining is concerned. They have never wanted anything from any government. All they want is to live their ojrn lives and to be dealt with fairly by government in matters of taxation.
One cannot visualize the government's going into mining. Let us picture the government spending the public's money and then, after a year or two of functioning, finding out that the venture was not what had been expected, with the result that the property would be left as it was in the first instance, possibly after losing a million dollars. Let us remember that in Flin Flon private capital and private enterprise spent about $30 million before it was in a position to produce.
What can the government do? Will it spend $30 million on a venture? Let us suppose that it does venture, and does spend $30 million on something which proves to be a fizzle, on a property where the ore bed did not measure up to expectations, and where the country has to spend large sums of money for nothing. These are the things we must remember when we think of mining.
Let- me say this, too, that governments have very few qualities of human beings, but very many of their faults-and that applies to all governments. For instance, let us consider nazism. Would any citizen of any country of his own initiative, through the activities of a single man, allow youth to be destroyed by the millions and tens of millions? That is what is done by governments. Can you visualize, for instance, what would have happened in England if there had been nationalization of industry at the time of the invention of the steam engine and the internal combustion engine? Can you visualize the government investing $5,000,000,000 to replace equipment that would be discarded almost overnight? It has never been done and it will never be done.
I repeat that I believe implicitly in the closest possible cooperation. Of necessity we must revolutionize our capitalistic system, but in doing that the workers will have to make some sacrifices, management will have to make sacrifices, and every citizen of this country will have to make sacrifices in order to make it a going concern.
You will never hear a whisper of a strike from the workers or farmers in Russia. I am not here to discuss communism or the internal IMr. Bradette.]
policies of that wonderful country, but no one can make me believe that in Russia they enjoy the same liberties that are enjoyed in Canada or in other sections of the world. The Russian government has instilled into the minds of its people the necessity of sacrifice by everyone for the good of the whole, and they are doing it. We will never deprive the workers of their right to strike when it is necessary to strike. More than that, we will never deprive any section of our population of full access to our governmental machinery. But even in times like the present, every section of the population must be prepared to make some sacrifice in order that we may arrive at a solution of the problems of peace.
I should like to give a few figures in connection with metal production in Ontario in 1941. Of the mineral production 76-4 per cent was derived from mineral areas discovered prior to 1910. We have to be careful with our mining industry. We do not want to destroy it. Some of the older mining fields have been worked out. The hon. member for Cape Breton South has referred to places in which there are ramshackle buildings, but those are in districts in which the mines have been worked out. Some hon. members may remember the old town of Cobalt, although many are too young to have seen it in its best days. In the past few-years that district ihas been deteriorating because the mining is playing out. Of the mineral production 13-2 per cent was derived from mineral areas discovered between 1910 and 1920; 4-3 per cent was derived from mineral areas discovered between 1920 and 1930, and only 6-1 per cent was derived from mineral areas discovered since 1930. I am putting these figures on Hansard because I am afraid that a resolution of this kind may scare away some of the capital which is necessary for the development of our own section of the country.
I can remember when Mr. Howard Ferguson was minister of mines and forests for Ontario. He went over to the United States and was able to interest $16,000,000 worth of capital in the development of the natural resources of the province. Those men were willing to risk their money. Many risks have been taken in connection with mining. Mining is not wholly on a dividend basis. Hon. members will' probably be surprised to know that the Ontario records show that 2,800 claims were recorded during the period of 1907-41 inclusive for each company which paid one or more dividends. There was a total of 317 companies which reached production, but only 113 reached the taxpaying stage in any amount. Only 1-8

per cent of some 4,426 organizations formed for precious metal mining were sufficiently successful to make any return whatsoever to their shareholders. It will be noted in this connection that not all of this 1-8 per cent could be considered to have been economically successful.
Before concluding i should like to make a few remarks about private and public enterprise. I come from a section of the country in which we have had to stand on our own feet as far as development is concerned. We could never have developed our forests and our mines if we had had to wait for the government of the day, whoever they might have been, to carry on this development. I have always been in favour of the Ontario hydro, but I should like to make a statement which may astonish some hon. members. I have farmed and resided in northern Ontario, in the Cochrane district, for nearly forty years, and still we have not the benefit of the Ontario hydro. During that period the provincial treasury has paid 810,000,000 to subsidize rural lines in southern Ontario. I have no quarrel with that because I am perfectly satisfied that the farmers of southern Ontario should enjoy the full benefit of the Ontario hydro, but we in the north country have helped to pay for the hydro lines in southern Ontario and we receive no benefits. I can remember going to Toronto and appearing before the hydro commission to inquire what they were going to do about providing hydro for our part of the country and I was always given the answer that the field was too speculative.
The fine industrial town of Kapuskasing was built by private enterprise. The Porcupine and Kirkland Lake districts, the Rouyn-Noranda district, and the Sudbury district, were all developed by private capital and private enterprise. These private enterprises have paid taxes into the provincial treasury, which taxes have helped to support the Ontario hydro. I am not criticizing that; besides, this is not the time to go too deeply into that matter. However, I want hon. members to know that the Ontario hydro has paid no taxes whereas the private corporations have.
Private enterprise took its money into the wilderness and gambled with it. Private enterprise has had to pay all the taxes I have mentioned. Only two years ago the Ontario hydro expropriated the Northern Power Company at Timmins and immediately the town of Timmins found itself short $35,000 in municipal taxes. I want hon. members to realize that it is not all so golden and rosy as some
people would have us believe. If we had had to wait for the Ontario hydro to develop northern Ontario, we would be waiting yet.
There must be cooperation between private enterprise and governmental activities, but I do not believe, nor do I think the majority of Canadian people believe, that the solution of the problems of this country will be arrived at by socializing our mining and other industries, and eventually our land. If you socialize one section of the national activities, you must socialize others. I should like to quote. H. D. Ainley, of the C.C.F. who said:
The C.C.F. has considered socialization of land. . . There are many advantages to the farmer from some form of socialism . . . We can learn much from Russia in this respect . . . Social security cannot be obtained as long as we leave control of our production in the hands of private individuals.
That is going pretty far. I believe if that language were repeated to the western farmers they would not fall in with such a system.
What is the hon. gentleman reading?
I am quoting Mr. H. D. Ainley.
Never heard of him.
Mr. H. D. Ainley on agricultural policy.
He is a private member of the organization. We do not smother people's views if they want to express them.
Yesterday evening it was not the same thing.
I did not smother his views; I repudiated them.

Here is another statement by the C.C.F.:
We cannot definitely state how much land a man will be allowed to hold. We propose that land .socialization shall be voluntary.
Who said that?

That is from the C.C.F. Saskatchewan farmer-labour group hand book, 1933. Then the following statement was made at the annual convention of the British Columbia C.C.F. on April 17, 1943:
Collective agriculture by the institution of methods of collective farming, such as have featured Soviet Russia's system, and by the creation of a provincial government monopoly in the purchase, processing and wholesaling of farm products, both those grown here and those imported.
These are definite words. I am just quoting them to the house to make hon. members realize that, once you get started you cannot
Mineral Resources

stop half-way. Natural resources belong primarily to the provinces. If the resolution were adopted by the government there would immediately be conflict with the provinces. The provincial premiers, the premier of Ontario, the premier of Quebec and the premier of Saskatchewan, who are always ready to fight for provincial rights, would be among the first to protest against such nationalization. I know the ability and energy and honesty of purpose of the premier of Saskatchewan because I have listened to him for years in this house. No one can doubt his sincerity of purpose but even he has not honesty of purpose of the premier of Saskatchewan. He has picked out a few industries but has not extended the field of socialization to mining. He has not even yet expropriated land for collective farming. I know enough of the -western farmers to know that the moment any government sought to introduce collective farming there would be a terrific revolt because every farmer wants to own his own farm. No one can tell me that the western farmers are ready for socialization of farming.
They do not have to be socialized because in this country a few people do not own all the land. The land is already socialized through individual ownership.

That is only a relative statement. The hon. member, who is so capable, knows that I may have a mortgage on my home or a farmer may have a mortgage on his farm, and while the law might compel me to pay the mortgage, no government has the right to interfere with the property.
Nobody wants to.

The same principle
applies to farms owned by the farmers of the west. They may have obligations on their land; but the land is theirs; their home is theirs, and even the King of England has no right to enter without permission. But under socialization it would be entirely, different. Let us be fair. You cannot call it fish at one time and flesh at another; it must be the same at all times. Our problems are great and difficult, but I believe in the intelligence of our people. I believe that in this parliament and in our provincial legislatures it will be possible to find a solution of all our problems.
In conclusion, I just wish to say how grateful I am personally-and this applies to my section of the country

for the spirit in which the premiers of the provinces met with the dominion last year to discuss dominion-provincial relations. No part of this country is

greater than the whole. Every member of this parliament is primarily a municipalist; that is, we believe in our own little town or big town, as the case may be, in our rural sections. Secondly, we are provincialists. But over and above all that, we stand for this wonderful country which is Canada, and I hope that when the premiers meet the dominion again the same spirit will animate them which prevailed' -in the last two conferences. That will be one of the best signs that we are going to develop into a still greater and better Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to follow the argument of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) because he dealt with coal mining. The resolution however, distinctly refers to the mineral resources of Canada, and that is the subject with which I wish to deal.
In my time I have had a lot to do with minerals of one kind and another, and I am familiar with all the difficulties experienced by prospectors, geologists and engineers in the discovery and opening up of our mineral resources. If what they have done could be written up it would be a romantic saga of their achievements.
The mining industry has been one of the great industries of Canada. I do not say that it is the greatest but it is one of our very great industries. It is one industry that has done a major job in opening up this country. If I may turn to the resolution for a moment it says:
Whereas private enterprise in the development of the mineral resources of Canada has not operated in the best interests of all of the people of Canada either in time of peace or in time of war . . .
That is a very broad statement which could not possibly be proved in any way. I am opposed to the resolution because I am in favour of private enterprise and private initiative. I have seen in my lifetime the marvellous achievements of private enterprise and private initiative, and my opinion based on that experience is that it would be impossible to have much initiative or enterprise in the mining industry if it were taken over by the government. The achievements of the mining industry are the result of private enterprise and private initiative. I think of the men I have met in the far north, the prospectors, and what they went through, how they had to endure the black flies, or bulldogs as they called them, and huge mosquitoes, grandfather and grandmother mosquitoes as they called them, when there
